# Registering on PROSPERO and risk of bias

A dose-response protocol has to commit to choices that a standard protocol never
mentions. This chapter walks the registration field by field, then rates the
studies it will include: both belong to the same class, because the protocol is
where the risk of bias plan is declared and declaring it later is not a plan.

## Why register a dose-response review

What pre-registration protects against when the analysis has many defensible
shapes.

## The fields that differ from a standard review

Exposure definition, dose scale, and the planned functional form.

## Committing to a model before seeing the data

Declaring two-stage or one-stage, the spline basis, and the knot placement in
advance, and how to phrase a contingency without writing a blank cheque.

## Declaring the dose metric

The unit, the reference level, and how open-ended categories will be assigned.

## Planned sensitivity analyses

Which modelling choices will be varied, and which results would change the
conclusion.

## A worked record

The registration for the physical activity review [@garcia2023] read as a model
to copy.

## Why risk of bias is part of the protocol

A rating scheme chosen after seeing the studies is a rating scheme chosen to get
an answer. The protocol is the only place it costs nothing to commit.

## Picking a tool for the designs you have

Dose-response reviews are usually built from cohorts, so ROBINS-E rather than
RoB 2. What changes when a trial arm sneaks into the set.

## Rating a study, domain by domain

Confounding, exposure measurement, missing data, and the domains that bite hardest
when the exposure is a dose rather than a group.

## Exposure measurement is the domain that matters most

A mismeasured dose does not blur the curve evenly; it flattens it. Why this
domain outranks the others here.

## Carrying the ratings into the analysis

Pre-specifying the high-risk sensitivity analysis, and how the ratings feed the
GRADE assessment rather than sitting in a supplementary table.
